name: William Shakespeare
info: William Shakespeare (1564–1616) was an English playwright, poet and actor from Stratford-upon-Avon who wrote most of his known plays and poems between 1589 and 1613 and was a part-owner of the Lord Chamberlain's Men, later the King's Men.

facts.born: Stratford-upon-Avon, Warwickshire; baptised on 26 April 1564, his date of birth unknown but traditionally observed on 23 April; son of John Shakespeare, an alderman and glover, and Mary Arden
facts.died: 23 April 1616, at the age of 52, in Stratford-upon-Avon; no extant contemporary source explains how or why he died; buried in the chancel of Holy Trinity Church two days later
facts.role: Playwright, poet and actor; sharer in the Lord Chamberlain's Men (from the 1590s) and the King's Men (from 1603); part-owner of the Globe (1599); his company also took over the Blackfriars theatre in 1608
facts.known: some 39 plays, among them Hamlet, Othello, King Lear, Macbeth, Romeo and Juliet and The Tempest; 154 sonnets; the narrative poems Venus and Adonis and The Rape of Lucrece; the Globe; the First Folio of 1623, published after his death

t: Born and raised in Stratford-upon-Avon, Shakespeare was a known figure in the London theatre by 1592 and became an actor, writer and part-owner of the leading playing company, which gave him a large estate.
He wrote comedies and histories in the 1590s, mainly tragedies until 1608 and romances in his last phase, and appears to have retired to Stratford around 1613, three years before his death.
Few records of his private life survive, so his religion, his sexuality and his appearance have been argued over, and his friends Heminges and Condell published his plays in the First Folio of 1623.
dyk: The Globe burned to the ground on 29 June 1613 when a cannon fired during a performance of Henry VIII set fire to the thatch, an event that pinpoints the date of a Shakespeare play with rare precision.

sections.early:
William Shakespeare was the son of John Shakespeare, an alderman and a successful glover originally from Snitterfield in Warwickshire, and Mary Arden, the daughter of an affluent landowning family that was influential in the Recusant Catholic community. He was baptised in Stratford-upon-Avon on 26 April 1564. His date of birth is unknown but is traditionally observed on 23 April, Saint George's Day; the date can be traced to William Oldys and George Steevens, and has appealed to biographers because Shakespeare died on the same date in 1616. He was the third of eight children and the eldest surviving son.

No attendance records survive, but most biographers agree that he was probably educated at the King's New School in Stratford, a free school chartered in 1553 and based in the town's guildhall, about a quarter-mile from his home. Its curriculum would have given an intensive education in grammar based upon Latin classical authors.

At 18 he married 26-year-old Anne Hathaway. The consistory court of the Diocese of Worcester issued a marriage licence on 27 November 1582, and the Worcester chancellor allowed the banns to be read once instead of the usual three times, so the ceremony may have been arranged in some haste. Susanna was baptised on 26 May 1583, six months after the marriage; the twins Hamnet and Judith were baptised on 2 February 1585. Hamnet died of unknown causes at the age of 11 and was buried on 11 August 1596.
sections.rise:
After the birth of the twins Shakespeare left few historical traces until he was mentioned as part of the London theatre scene in 1592. Scholars call the years between 1585 and 1592 his "lost years". Biographers have reported many apocryphal stories. Nicholas Rowe, his first biographer, recounted a Stratford legend that he fled to London to escape prosecution for deer poaching on the estate of the squire Thomas Lucy; another 18th-century story has him minding theatre patrons' horses; John Aubrey reported that he had been a country schoolmaster. Little evidence substantiates such stories other than hearsay collected after his death.

By 1592 several of his plays were on the London stage, and he was known well enough to be attacked in print by the playwright Robert Greene in Groats-Worth of Wit as an "upstart Crow, beautified with our feathers" and "the only Shake-scene in a country". Most scholars agree that Greene accused him of reaching above his rank in trying to match university-educated writers such as Christopher Marlowe and Thomas Nashe. It is the earliest surviving mention of Shakespeare's work in the theatre.

After 1594 his plays were performed only by the Lord Chamberlain's Men, a company owned by a group of players, Shakespeare among them, that soon became the leading company in London. Some of his plays appeared in quarto editions from 1594, and by 1598 his name had become a selling point on the title pages. In 1593 and 1594, with the theatres closed because of plague, he published the narrative poems Venus and Adonis and The Rape of Lucrece, dedicated to Henry Wriothesley, 3rd Earl of Southampton.
sections.deeds:
Shakespeare produced most of his known works between 1589 and 1613; his extant works, including collaborations, consist of some 39 plays, 154 sonnets, 3 long narrative poems and a few other verses. The first recorded works are Richard III and the three parts of Henry VI, written in the early 1590s. The mid-1590s brought the comedies A Midsummer Night's Dream, The Merchant of Venice, Much Ado About Nothing, As You Like It and Twelfth Night, and the histories Richard II, Henry IV and Henry V; Romeo and Juliet and Julius Caesar, based on Sir Thomas North's 1579 translation of Plutarch, begin and end the period. In the early 17th century he wrote the "problem plays" and the tragedies Hamlet, Othello, King Lear and Macbeth, and in his last phase the romances Cymbeline, The Winter's Tale and The Tempest, then collaborations including Henry VIII and The Two Noble Kinsmen, probably with John Fletcher.

In 1599 a partnership of members of the company built the Globe on the south bank of the Thames, and in 1608 the company also took over the Blackfriars indoor theatre. After Elizabeth's death in 1603 the company received a royal patent from James I and became the King's Men. Shakespeare also acted in his own and other plays. His association with the company made him a wealthy man: in 1597 he bought New Place, the second-largest house in Stratford, and in 1605 he invested in a share of the parish tithes there. The Sonnets, published in 1609, were the last of his non-dramatic works to be printed.
sections.opponents:
Shakespeare was attacked in his own time and judged unevenly afterwards. Robert Greene's jibe of 1592 was the first. Ben Jonson, who hailed him in the First Folio as "Soul of the age", remarked elsewhere that "Shakespeare wanted art", meaning that he lacked skill. Between the Restoration in 1660 and the end of the 17th century, when classical ideas were in vogue, critics mostly rated him below John Fletcher and Ben Jonson, and Thomas Rymer condemned him for mixing the comic with the tragic. George Bernard Shaw mocked the cult of Shakespeare worship as "bardolatry", claiming that Henrik Ibsen's new naturalism had made Shakespeare obsolete.

Some of the plays trouble modern audiences. In The Two Gentlemen of Verona two friends appear to approve of rape, and the taming of a woman's independent spirit by a man in The Taming of the Shrew sometimes troubles critics and directors. The Merchant of Venice portrays the vengeful Jewish moneylender Shylock in a way that reflects dominant Elizabethan views but may appear derogatory to modern audiences.

About 230 years after his death doubts began to be expressed about the authorship of the works. Proposed alternative candidates include Francis Bacon, Christopher Marlowe and Edward de Vere, 17th Earl of Oxford. All but a few Shakespeare scholars and literary historians consider the theory fringe. His private religious views have also been debated: he conformed to the official state religion, but some scholars hold that members of his family were Catholics, at a time when practising Catholicism was against the law, while others argue that the evidence is lacking.
sections.last:
Nicholas Rowe was the first biographer to record the tradition, repeated by Samuel Johnson, that Shakespeare retired to Stratford "some years before his death". He was still working as an actor in London in 1608, and he continued to visit London in the years 1611–1614: in 1612 he was called as a witness in the case of Bellott v Mountjoy, and in March 1613 he bought a gatehouse in the former Blackfriars priory. After 1610 he wrote fewer plays and none are attributed to him after 1613. His last three plays were collaborations, probably with John Fletcher, who succeeded him as house playwright of the King's Men.

Shakespeare died on 23 April 1616, at the age of 52, within a month of signing his will, which begins by describing him as being in "perfect health". No extant contemporary source explains how or why he died. Half a century later John Ward, the vicar of Stratford, wrote in his notebook that Shakespeare, Michael Drayton and Ben Jonson had "a merry meeting" and that Shakespeare "died of a fever there contracted". He was survived by his wife and two daughters, Susanna, who had married the physician John Hall in 1607, and Judith, who had married Thomas Quiney two months before his death. Shakespeare was buried in the chancel of Holy Trinity Church two days after he died.

He left the bulk of his large estate to Susanna, on condition that she pass it down intact to "the first son of her body". He left his wife Anne "my second best bed", a bequest that some scholars see as an insult and others as a gift of the marital bed, rich in significance. The Halls' only child, Elizabeth, died without children in 1670, ending his direct line.
sections.legacy:
In 1623 John Heminges and Henry Condell, fellow actors and friends of Shakespeare's, published the First Folio, a collected edition of his plays with 36 texts, 18 of them printed for the first time. Many had already appeared in quartos of varying quality, which the Folio called "stol'n and surreptitious copies". Jonson's poem in its preface said that Shakespeare was "not of an age, but for all time". A funerary monument with a half-effigy of him in the act of writing had been erected on the north wall of Holy Trinity Church before 1623. No written description of his appearance survives, and some scholars take the Droeshout engraving, which Jonson approved as a good likeness, and the Stratford monument as the best evidence of it.

Critical opinion rose over the 18th century. Samuel Johnson's edition of 1765 and Edmond Malone's of 1790 added to his reputation, and by 1800 he was firmly enshrined as the national poet, the "Bard of Avon". Voltaire, Goethe, Stendhal and Victor Hugo championed him abroad. Christoph Martin Wieland was the first to produce complete translations of the plays in any language, and the plays have since been translated into over 80 languages. Thomas Carlyle wrote in 1840 of "This King Shakespeare" shining over us all.

His use of language helped to shape modern English: Johnson quoted him more often than any other author in his Dictionary, and phrases such as "with bated breath" and "a foregone conclusion" passed into everyday speech. Scholars have identified 20,000 pieces of music linked to his works, among them Verdi's operas Macbeth, Otello and Falstaff, and Akira Kurosawa adapted Macbeth and King Lear as Throne of Blood and Ran. Sigmund Freud drew on Hamlet for his theories of human nature.

summary: William Shakespeare (1564–1616), born in Stratford-upon-Avon, became an actor, playwright and part-owner of the Lord Chamberlain's Men, later the King's Men. He wrote comedies, histories, tragedies, romances and poems, and his plays were collected in the First Folio of 1623, seven years after his death.

G.E. Bentley, Shakespeare: A Biographical Handbook (Yale University Press, 1986)
E.K. Chambers, William Shakespeare: A Study of Facts and Problems (Clarendon Press, 1988)
